Upgraded vision encoder shared between FSD, Robotaxi, and Optimus, which is trained on millions of internet videos for improved generalization and data efficiency, improving the critical intervention rate by 25x.

Flashback to June 14, 2024.

At the time, frontier AI models have zero fluid intelligence. They score around 5% on ARC 1. They can't reliably add two numbers. They make laughable logic errors every other prompt. Reasoning models don't exist. Coding agents don't exist. Claude Code doesn't exist. "Code gen" is a complete joke. Scaling up next-token prediction based on web text data is hitting a wall.

What if a time traveler told you that, by November 2026...

• AI models would have human-like fluid intelligence, thanks to a new paradigm: test-time induction (modern reasoning models).
• Not only would ARC 1 be saturated, but unreleased benchmarks 10x harder (ARC 2) and 100x harder (ARC 3) would be saturated too.
• Nearly all code would be written by AI, and models could one-shot complex codebases flawlessly.
• AI models would be solving multiple Millennium Prize problems.
• OpenAI's valuation would be 15x higher, and Anthropic's would be 85x higher.

And on top of all that...

• Nvidia would still hold ~80% of the AI compute market.
• Nvidia would have grown its revenue and earnings 4.5x.
• Nvidia would still be growing 75% a year.
• Nvidia would have even higher operating margins (67% vs. 65% back then).

Based on that information, straight from the future, would you have bought NVDA?

If you answered yes -- congrats. Today, 2.5 years later, you'd be down 5% on your investment (even more after inflation).

Starlink is transforming a remote mountain water gate in Japan that sits completely outside mobile network coverage

For years, workers had to travel roughly 35 minutes along a dangerous mountain road just to inspect the facility. During heavy rain, floods, or at night, reaching the site became even more dangerous

Now KDDI and Japanese farm-tech company farmo have connected the Shinbori headworks in Sekikawa, Niigata, using Starlink Mini

Here's how the system works:

• Starlink Mini provides satellite internet where cellular networks don't reach

• LoRa connects water-level sensors and the automated water gate

• Solar panels power the equipment where grid electricity is difficult to access

• Cloud monitoring gives operators real-time water levels, camera feeds, equipment status, and emergency alerts

• Workers remotely open and close the water gate without physically visiting the site

The results are already impressive:

All 6 remote gate-control tests were SUCCESSFUL

Workers now have visibility and control over infrastructure that previously required a dangerous mountain trip just to inspect

This becomes especially important during floods and emergencies, when every minute matters and sending workers into dangerous conditions puts lives at risk

The project will continue in Japan's FY2027, with plans to expand into automated water management, disaster prevention, and other agricultural applications

This is another example of what Starlink is making possible

Starlink just secured another major spectrum expansion in Brazil, and the authorization is now OFFICIAL 🇧🇷

Brazil's telecom regulator Anatel published Act No. 14,179 on November 19, formally adding new radio-frequency bands to Starlink's existing satellite authorization

• 4 new downlink frequency sub-bands
• Additional spectrum across Ku, Ka and Q/V bands
• Authorization covering ALL of Brazil
• Non-exclusive use for the remaining term of Starlink's existing authorization
• Approved by Anatel's board in October and formally published November 19

The authorization is held by Space Exploration Holdings, with Starlink Brazil Holding serving as its local representative

These additional frequencies are an important part of expanding Starlink's satellite communications capacity and supporting its next-generation network

And with Starlink V3 satellites bringing dramatically more bandwidth per satellite, securing additional spectrum is very important

Brazil is already a major market for Starlink, and SpaceX is continuing to build the regulatory foundation for its future expansion

Step by step, Starlink is securing the infrastructure and spectrum needed to keep scaling across Brazil

On Starship’s 15th flight last week, the Super Heavy booster correctly performed a safe abort when returning for a catch and ended its mission with a splashdown in the water off the coast of Starbase. Following splashdown, SpaceX recovery teams were immediately onsite to safe the area while our Environmental Health and Safety team worked to ensure any debris that washes onshore was recovered → http://x.com/SpaceX/status/2121629958036492590

When we received reports of potential debris in Mexican territory, we immediately mobilized to send specialists to aid in identification and lead any cleanup work required, just as we did on Boca Chica Beach near Starbase. We continue to stay in contact with the Mexican government and are on standby to send support if authorities in Mexico tell us it is actually needed. Partners on the ground relayed that theyhave found very little debris in their sweeps of the beach, and the small amount they have found are not clearly from SpaceX operations.

The majority of the social media posts online claiming widespread debris and damage are either outright fabrications or intentionally misleading. Elon Musk explains why SpaceX catching Starship achieves the "holy grail of rocketry," and can cut the cost of access to space by 100x:

In 2025, SpaceX launched 2,200 tons to orbit, more than 80% of the global total.

Elon Musk's goal with Starship is 1,000,000 tons to orbit per year, about 450x what SpaceX launched last year.

Falcon 9 reuses its booster but throws away the upper stage on every flight. Starship is designed to bring back both.

"We've had three booster catches, but this is the first ship catch, which means we've now at least proven that all parts of Starship can be flown to space and recovered in good enough shape to be reflown."

"No one has ever taken a stage like that and created a truly reusable upper stage, and certainly not brought it back and had it land propulsively while being caught by giant chopsticks, which sounds like some kind of preposterous sci-fi book or something. But it's done."

"Starship can drop the cost of access to space by a factor of 100... and achieve a mass to orbit rate that is in the million ton per year range."

"This has been the holy grail of rocketry from the beginning, to have a fully reusable rocket system."

"The Space Shuttle was partially reusable, but the main tank… was thrown away on every flight… The shuttle orbiter, the plane-like thing, would take something like nine months to refurbish between flights."

"Whereas Starship is designed for complete reusability and to be reused immediately like an airplane. The booster lands, you can put another ship on top and take off immediately."

"The net effect of this, to put it into economic terms, is a hundredfold reduction in the cost of access to space, and maybe even eventually a thousandfold reduction."

"That's what's necessary in order to make life multiplanetary, in order to build a city on the Moon or Mars… You couldn't do it even if you had the whole budget of the United States government."

Elon Musk and SpaceX have been working toward a fully reusable orbital rocket for more than two decades.

Five days ago, they proved every part of Starship can fly to space and be recovered.

quote.author: firesidealpha

quote.text:
Dario Amodei says Anthropic could drive at 200 miles an hour but chooses 90

“So this is one of the central tensions at the heart of the company, but it’s really because this technology is so powerful, it has so many effects in the world. It’s something that every company in this space will have to face, whether they want to or not. We’re just facing it more explicitly and more thoughtfully. And so you think about something like pacing.”

“The idea behind pacing was, imagine that you’re driving your car at 60 miles an hour, and then you discover or invent something that could let you drive the car at 200 miles an hour. This is models building themselves, recursive self-improvement. What we’ve done with pacing is essentially said, look, we could drive at 200 miles an hour. Maybe let’s only drive at 90 miles an hour. Spend time figuring out how to do that safely, and the rest of that surplus, we spend building the model in the right way.”

“And I think in the long run, that will work out pretty well for the investors as well, because the company that builds the safest, that has the trust of the customers and the enterprises of the world, I think that is the company that’s going to be both best for society and, in the long run, I hope, best for the performance of the company.”

Back in 2016, Elon Musk laid out the scale of what it would actually take to build a self-sustaining city on Mars

The goal was to build a civilization that can survive on its own

The scale Elon laid out:

• ~100 people per ship  
• Mars launch opportunities roughly every 2 years
• Around 10,000 trips to move 1 million people  
• A spacecraft large enough to carry people, luggage and massive amounts of cargo  

At the time, the hardest part was obvious:

You needed a transportation system that can fly again and again

Now that future is getting much closer

Starship has returned from space and been caught by the tower

The next step is rapid reuse, reflying the same ship again and again until spaceflight starts looking more like aviation

In 2016, Elon described the transportation system needed to build a city on Mars

In 2026, SpaceX is finally starting to prove the reusability that makes it possible
